final_proof:
Let \(s[P]=\{s(x):x\in P\}\). We use the defining properties of a Peano structure that \(0\in P\), that \(s:P\to P\), that \(0\notin s[P]\), and the induction axiom: if \(A\subseteq P\), \(0\in A\), and \(s[A]\subseteq A\), then \(A=P\).

Set
\[
A=\{0\}\cup s[P].
\]
Because \(0\in P\) and \(s[P]\subseteq P\), we have \(A\subseteq P\). Certainly \(0\in A\). Moreover, if \(a\in A\), then \(a\in P\), so \(s(a)\in s[P]\subseteq A\). Hence \(s[A]\subseteq A\). The induction axiom therefore gives
\[
P=A=\{0\}\cup s[P].
\]

Now let \(x\in P\setminus s[P]\). From the displayed equality, either \(x=0\) or \(x\in s[P]\). The second alternative contradicts the choice of \(x\), so \(x=0\). Thus
\[
P\setminus s[P]\subseteq\{0\}.
\]
Conversely, \(0\in P\) and the Peano axiom \(0\notin s[P]\) imply \(0\in P\setminus s[P]\). Consequently
\[
P\setminus s[P]=\{0\}.
\]
Since \(\{0\}\) is a singleton, \(P\setminus s[P]\) is a singleton, and \(0\) is the unique non-successor element of \(P\).
